member.name: F:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateBorrowStrategy.Lifo
member.summary:

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateCircuitBreakerOptions
member.summary: Circuit-breaker settings for the pool-level availability guard, used when is on.
member.remarks: The breaker protects the pool as a whole rather than an individual object. When the dependency behind the pool fails, the application reports it with SetUnavailable; once the configured number of consecutive failures has accumulated, the pool marks itself unavailable and every further acquire fails immediately instead of handing out objects that are likely to be broken. While unavailable, a background probe runs on the pool's shared timer — the probe is the only background work the breaker adds, it starts only when the breaker trips and stops as soon as the pool recovers.

member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateCircuitBreakerOptions.FailureThreshold
member.summary:
Number of consecutive reported dependency failures that trips the breaker.
Default value: (3).
member.remarks:
Purpose: absorbs transient hiccups — a single failure report does not take the pool out of service.
Special case: the streak counts consecutive reports without an intervening recovery. It is reset to 0 by SetAvailable (explicitly, or through a successful probe), so a pool that recovered needs repeated fresh failures before it trips again; sporadic failures spread over a healthy lifetime also accumulate, and an application that knows the dependency is fine can call SetAvailable at any time to clear the pending streak. Set it to 1 to trip on the first report.
Boundary: values below 1 are normalized to 1 by .

member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateCircuitBreakerOptions.ResetTimeout
member.remarks:
Purpose: gives the failing dependency room to recover without being probed on every tick. No probe runs during this window, so a short value is safe but increases the probe rate against a dependency that is still down.
Boundary: values <= are normalized to the default.

member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateCircuitBreakerOptions.ProbeInterval
member.remarks:
Purpose: bounds how long the pool stays unavailable after the dependency recovers. This is also the resolution at which the probe is scheduled, because it is the only period the breaker contributes to the shared background timer.
Boundary: values <= are normalized to the default.

member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateCircuitBreakerOptions.Probe
member.summary: The background probe that decides whether the dependency is healthy again. Default null.
member.remarks:
Return true to bring the pool back into service — the pool then closes the breaker and raises ; return false to stay unavailable and be probed again after the next . The delegate runs on the pool's background timer, never on a borrow or return path, and an exception it throws is caught and logged as a failed probe.
When this is null no automatic recovery happens: the pool stays unavailable until the application calls SetAvailable, which is the right choice when only the caller can know that the dependency is back.

member.summary:
Borrow lease context (2.5, breaking change).
One borrow corresponds to one immutable lease context: a process-wide monotonically increasing lease id, a borrow-time timestamp (Stopwatch ticks), and a borrow-frame array. The carrier is (): the context flows with the caller's asynchronous execution flow (ExecutionContext), and concurrent borrows and returns each hold an independent copy, so they no longer overwrite each other (in 2.4 and earlier, string-based capture on the wrapper object was overwritten by re-borrows of the same object, and could not be attributed correctly across asynchronous flows when shared).

Purpose: for pure pooling workloads — objects that need no validation, eviction, leak forensics, metrics or auto-scaling — the pool can store the pooled value directly in a bounded array and borrow/return it through Interlocked operations. That removes the per-object wrapper allocation, the per-shard free-list lock, the registry lookup on return and every diagnostic call from the borrow/return path.
Special case: lean is a mode, not a knob — enabling it forces , , , , , , , and off and clears the capacity-alarm thresholds, because each of them needs per-object bookkeeping or a background timer that the fast path does not maintain. The normalized result is produced by (also called from ) and is visible through the pool's GetOptions. Ordering is therefore irrelevant: WithLean() followed by WithEnableMetrics(true) still ends up in lean mode.
Consequences to be aware of: the lean path keeps no cumulative counters ( and friends report 0), rejects , cannot resize its retention buffer through ReloadConfig, and trusts the caller of Release to hand back an object that really came from this pool.
